idiom_name: sealed approval states + JVM method security (@PreAuthorize / AuthorizationManager) over the authenticated principal
implementation_notes: Kotlin inherits the JVM's enforcement machinery - Spring Security method security on the JVM, or Ktor's authenticate/authorize plugins on Kotlin-first services - so the principal is read from the security context and the distinct-approver predicate is a policy expression or a guard around the release operation. What Kotlin adds locally is the state model: a sealed interface hierarchy (Pending, Approved, Rejected) combined with when-expressions makes exhaustive handling of the workflow states a compile-time property, so a new state cannot be introduced without revisiting every transition (the sealed-class guarantee the Kotlin documentation describes). What neither the language nor the framework supplies is the identity rule itself - the approver's stable id compared with the stored initiator - so that check must sit at the enforcement point, not in a UI flow.
pitfalls: A sealed state machine proves the transitions, not who performs them; the distinct-approver check stays a runtime predicate that no second code path may bypass.
Spring Security annotations are inert unless method security is enabled (@EnableMethodSecurity) and the call goes through the proxy; self-invocation inside the same bean bypasses the interceptor.
Coroutines suspend across the check: do not hold a transaction or lock while awaiting a remote approval service, or the lock lifetime becomes the workflow lifetime.
